stories.headline: 30-YEAR TREASURY YIELD HITS HIGHEST SINCE 2002 AS RATE-HIKE BETS DEEPEN
stories.body: The 30-year Treasury yield pushed above 5.61% Tuesday, a level last seen in June 2002, while the 10-year held near 5.25% as the seven-month Iran war keeps fueling expectations the Fed will need to hike again to fight oil-driven inflation. The S&P 500 slipped 0.16% to 7,671 as the long end of the curve continued its multi-week climb.
stories.explain: The long end of the curve moves on term premium — the extra compensation investors demand for locking up money for 30 years — rather than on near-term Fed policy expectations alone, so a persistent war-driven inflation shock pushes 30-year yields higher even when short rates aren't moving as fast. Because higher long-term borrowing costs raise the discount rate applied to every future cash flow, from mortgages to corporate capex to equity valuations, a multi-decade high here tightens financial conditions well beyond what the Fed funds rate alone would suggest.

stories.headline: OIL EASES SLIGHTLY BUT STAYS ELEVATED AS IRAN REJECTS U.S. TERMS ON HORMUZ
stories.body: WTI crude slipped 2.3% to around $90 a barrel Tuesday, cooling modestly after Monday's spike, but remains near multi-month highs after Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Iranian officials have privately signaled they don't expect a deal before U.S. midterm elections in November, keeping a war risk premium baked into crude.
stories.explain: Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption transits the Strait of Hormuz, so futures price the probability-weighted risk of a prolonged closure, not just today's actual flow of barrels — a small easing in tension lets some of that premium unwind even without any change in physical supply. Because energy costs feed directly into headline CPI and corporate input costs, the price of oil is functioning right now as a real-time gauge of the market's confidence in a near-term Iran resolution.

stories.headline: ANTHROPIC TARGETS $2 TRILLION IPO VALUATION DESPITE $42 BILLION 2025 LOSS
stories.body: Anthropic is pushing toward an October public offering targeting a $2 trillion valuation — more than double its $965 billion private mark from May — even after reportedly posting $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue against a $42 billion loss. Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Citi are all underwriting the deal, one of the largest tech listings ever attempted.
stories.explain: A $2 trillion ask on $4.6 billion of revenue is roughly a 430x sales multiple, a number that can't be justified by current cash flows and instead rests entirely on assumptions about the growth rate and eventual margins many years out — which is why 12x revenue growth from 2024 matters more to bankers here than the current loss. That bet becomes riskier precisely when long-term discount rates are rising, since far-out projected profits get discounted more harshly the higher risk-free yields climb.

stories.headline: AMD'S $8.2B WORLD LABS DEAL AND ARM'S WILD SWING HIGHLIGHT CHOPPY TECH TAPE
stories.body: AMD shares rose over 1% after announcing an $8.2 billion all-stock acquisition of AI research firm World Labs to build out spatial-intelligence models, while Arm Holdings swung from an 8.7% intraday plunge to a 4.9% gain by the close. The Nasdaq 100 finished roughly flat at 30,250 as AI dealmaking offset broader rate-driven jitters.
stories.explain: An all-stock deal lets AMD pay for World Labs without touching cash or taking on debt at a moment when borrowing costs are near multi-decade highs, effectively using its own richly-valued shares as currency — a tactic more companies lean on when the cost of debt-financed M&A becomes prohibitive. Arm's violent round-trip shows how thinly-held, high-multiple AI names are especially sensitive to single-stock headlines right now, since a stretched valuation leaves little cushion against any negative catalyst.

stories.headline: GOLD REBOUNDS OFF SEVEN-WEEK LOW AS DOLLAR HOLDS NEAR TWO-MONTH HIGH
stories.body: Spot gold rose 1.1% to around $4,163 an ounce Tuesday, clawing back part of Monday's 3% slump, even as the Dollar Index (DXY) firmed to 101.37, near its highest level in two months, on continued rate-hike bets.
stories.explain: Gold's bounce here is a safe-haven bid reasserting itself after being overwhelmed by rising real yields on Monday, but the fact that it's rising alongside a strengthening dollar — normally an inverse relationship, since a pricier dollar makes gold costlier for foreign buyers — shows geopolitical demand is currently strong enough to offset that usual headwind. Watch which force wins if the Fed follows through on the hike markets are now pricing: further dollar strength would need to overcome that safe-haven bid for gold's rally to stall out again.

stories.headline: 100 DAYS FROM TIP-OFF: NEVADA'S STEVE ALFORD TO RETIRE, DUKE ADDS ON-COURT ADS
stories.body: With the 2026-27 season 101 days from its Notre Dame-Villanova opener in Rome, Nevada coach Steve Alford announced he'll retire at season's end after 36 years on the sideline, while Duke is rolling out on-court advertising at Cameron Indoor for the first time as programs lean further into NIL-era revenue streams.

stories.headline: NBA MEDIA DAY: LEBRON DEBUTS WITH SIXERS, JOKIC TEASES EXTENSION, VEGAS EXPANSION BIDS TOP $12B
stories.body: LeBron James spoke to media for the first time as a 76er, Kawhi Leonard did the same in Toronto, and Nikola Jokic said "I'm gonna sign next year, if they want me" on a new Nuggets deal, as all 30 teams held Media Day ahead of Tuesday's training camp openings. Separately, the NBA is reviewing finalist bids for a Las Vegas expansion team valued at $12-13 billion.

stories.headline: COMMANDERS' DANIELS AVOIDS ELBOW SURGERY FOR NOW AS GIANTS RELEASE BECKHAM
stories.body: Washington QB Jayden Daniels will hold off on surgery for his dislocated left elbow, though it could still happen after the season, while the Giants released WR Odell Beckham Jr. after just three games and 19 snaps following his offseason re-signing. Miami's De'Von Achane (season-ending ACL tear) and Tampa Bay's Jalen McMillan (6-8 week PCL injury) headline a heavy Week 3 injury toll.

stories.headline: AP POLL SHAKEUP: WISCONSIN STUNS NO. 6 PENN STATE, FLORIDA ROCKETS TO NO. 8
stories.body: Wisconsin erased a 10-point deficit with two late Colton Joseph touchdown passes to stun Penn State 24-20, knocking the Nittany Lions out of the rankings entirely, while Florida's 52-28 rout of then-No. 4 Ole Miss vaulted the Gators to No. 8. Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith became the program's first 3,000-yard career receiver in a 217-yard, 4-TD outing against Illinois.

Added Nevada transfer guard Tayshawn Comer and hired former Oregon assistant Mike Mennenga and GM Alex Kline this month. Big Ten released UW's 20-game league schedule (10 home, 10 away) on Sept. 16.

deepDive.title: Pricing a $2 Trillion IPO on $4.6 Billion of Revenue
content: Anthropic is pushing toward an October listing targeting a $2 trillion valuation — more than double its $965 billion private mark from just four months ago — despite reporting $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue against a $42 billion loss. That ask lands on the same day the 30-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since 2002, which is not a coincidence worth ignoring: the two numbers are directly in tension, because one measures how much investors will pay for cash flows that don't exist yet, and the other measures how expensive it has become to wait for them.

The mechanism is discounting. A $2 trillion price tag on $4.6 billion of revenue is roughly a 430x sales multiple, a number no discounted cash flow model can support using today's numbers — DCF breaks down here because near-term free cash flow is deeply negative and the entire valuation hinges on a terminal assumption decades out. Bankers instead lean on forward revenue multiples benchmarked against comparable hypergrowth software and AI companies, effectively outsourcing the discounting problem to whatever multiple the market is currently willing to pay, which is itself a function of prevailing interest rates.

What most people miss is that a pre-profit growth stock behaves like a long-dated zero-coupon bond: nearly all of its expected value sits far in the future, giving it very high interest-rate duration. A 1-point rise in the discount rate shaves far more off a cash flow promised in 2035 than off one promised next year, compounded over a decade-plus horizon. That's exactly what happened to unprofitable tech in 2021-2022, when the Fed's hiking cycle cut many high-multiple names in half even as their revenue kept growing — the cash flows hadn't changed, but the price of waiting for them had.

For Chris, the read-through is that Anthropic's $2 trillion number is really a bet that today's oil-and-war-driven yield spike proves temporary. If the 30-year keeps grinding toward its 2002 highs into October, bankers may find it harder to defend that multiple to institutional buyers, and the IPO could price below target or get delayed — the same pattern that hit Oura's listing today. Watch how comparable public AI names trade on revenue multiples over the next two weeks; that's the market's real-time verdict on whether $2 trillion survives contact with a 5.6% long bond.
